Empirical Research Plan  
“Child Penalty in Denmark: Causal Evidence on Long-Run Gender Gaps after the First Birth”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Event-study Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with individual fixed effects (a.k.a. dynamic DiD).  
• We treat the calendar year of the first child’s birth (t = 0) as the intervention.  
• We compare mothers to fathers who experience their first child in the same calendar year cohort, exploiting the fact that prior to parenthood men and women on average display very similar earnings trajectories in Denmark.  
• Individual FE remove all time-invariant heterogeneity; calendar-year FE absorb macro shocks; event-time dummies trace out dynamic effects up to 20 years after birth.  

Why appropriate  
• Large-scale, high-frequency administrative panel ⇒ precise event timing and long pre/post panels.  
• The “as-good-as-random” timing of conception conditional on couple characteristics and labor-market history is plausible in Denmark because contraception is widespread and income-conditioning of parental benefits is limited.  
• Using fathers in the same birth cohort controls for shocks related to the baby itself (household shock, fertility preferences, year-specific macro events, policy changes). The remaining gender differential isolates the causal “child penalty” borne by women.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = Female × (Post-birth). Formally, D_it = 1{Female_i = 1 & t ≥ 0}, where t=0 is first-birth year.

Control group  
Men who become fathers in the same birth-cohort year (t = 0 for them as well). They experience the same fertility shock, but Danish leave-taking norms imply they bear a much smaller career cost.

Treatment timing / key variation  
Event time k = −10,…,20 (10 years pre birth to 20 years post). The coefficients β_k on Female × 1{k} provide dynamic treatment effects; β_0 is the contemporaneous “impact”. The “long-run child penalty” is β_20.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of children, male and female prospective parents would have continued on parallel earnings paths.  
• Plausibility: Danish couples tend to assortatively mate on age & education; gender pay gaps pre-birth are small. Long pre-period data allow visual/ statistical validation.

A2. No gender-differential anticipation: Prospective mothers do not already cut back earnings *earlier* than fathers conditional on conception timing.  
• Plausibility: Pregnancy becomes public late; generous maternity benefits start only a few weeks before the due date.

A3. Stable composition: The set of men and women who give birth in a given year remains in the panel over time; attrition is not gender-differential.  
• Plausibility: Virtually no out-migration; mortality low; admin registers track individuals continuously.

A4. No other contemporaneous gender-targeted policy changes coincide exactly with first-birth timing.  
• Plausibility: Denmark’s parental-leave reforms are enacted nationwide on specific calendar years, not idiosyncratically with individual births. Calendar-year FE absorb those.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous timing of first birth (career-oriented women postpone childbirth).  
Mitigation:  
• Condition on detailed age-by-education fixed effects.  
• Instrumental-variables robustness: Use infertility shocks (IV = IVF treatments availability) on a subsample; results similar strengthen credibility.

T2. Fathers may also reduce labor supply (paternity leave uptake).  
Mitigation:  
• Measure and control for realized father leave days.  
• Alternatively, use a triple-difference: mothers vs fathers *and* earlier vs later cohorts around major paternity-leave expansions.

T3. Measurement error in birth timing (late registrations abroad, adoptions).  
Mitigation:  
• Restrict to biological children born in Denmark (civil registry date precise to the day).  
• Test robustness excluding adopters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#############################################################
# 0. Packages
#############################################################
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)      # event-study plots

#############################################################
# 1. Load data
#############################################################
# Assume three CSVs: persons, earnings, births
pers   <- fread("dk_persons.csv")        # id, sex, dob, education
earn   <- fread("dk_earnings.csv")       # id, year, wage_income
births <- fread("dk_births.csv")         # id_parent, date_birth_child

#############################################################
# 2. Construct first-birth event time
#############################################################
# keep only first child for each parent
births <- births[order(id_parent, date_birth_child)]
births <- births[ , .SD[1], by = id_parent]

# Merge
dt <- merge(earn, births, by.x = "id", by.y = "id_parent", all.x = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, pers, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)

# Event time (k = year relative to birth)
dt[, birth_year := year(date_birth_child)]
dt[, k := year - birth_year]                   # negative = pre

# Keep window −10..20 around birth and parents only
dt <- dt[k >= -10 & k <= 20 & !is.na(k)]

# Indicator variables
dt[, female := (sex == "F")]
dt[, post  := as.integer(k >= 0)]
dt[, treat := female * post]

#############################################################
# 3. Main event-study specification
#############################################################
# create event-time dummies interacted with female
dt[, k_fac := factor(k)]

# OLS with individual and calendar-year FE
es <- feols(wage_income ~ i(k, female, ref = -1) | id + year,
            data = dt, cluster = ~id)

summary(es)

# Event-study plot
plot_df <- coefplot(es, keep = "female", drop = "ref")$data
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = as.numeric(term), y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  labs(x = "Years relative to birth", y = "Earnings gap (log DKK)",
       title = "Dynamic child penalty: Female – Male")

#############################################################
# 4. Robustness: placebo on pre-treatment
#############################################################
# Fake treatment at k = -5
dt[, fake_post := as.integer(k >= -5)]
dt[, fake_treat := female * fake_post]

placebo <- feols(wage_income ~ fake_treat | id + year, data = dt,
                 cluster = ~id)
summary(placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: Mothers’ earnings will fall sharply relative to fathers starting at t = 0, stabilizing at −20 % to −30 % within 3 years and persisting for at least 10–20 years. Fathers’ earnings may rise slightly due to increased labor supply or employer perceptions, implying a combined gender gap of roughly −25 %.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = good, 0 = weak)
Parallel pre-trends tested and satisfied: 1  
No differential anticipation: 0.8  
Stable composition / attrition: 1  
Measurement accuracy of timing and outcomes: 1  
No simultaneous confounders (policy shocks, macro): 0.8  

Overall score ≈ 4.6 / 5 → high internal validity but still reliant on parallel trend and anticipation assumptions.
